sentences.text: Laueropterus possessed a wingspan of roughly one meter, distinguishing it as larger than most other early monofenestratans.
The skull of the holotype — the specimen the species is based on — measures approximately 20.5 centimeters in length.
Fossil remains were discovered around 2007 in the Schaudiberg Quarry near Mühlheim in Bavaria, Germany, and scientifically named in 2026.
The holotype was acquired by the Lauer Foundation in Illinois, United States, in January 2024, honoring René and Bruce Lauer for their work making Solnhofen fossils accessible to science.
The species name 'vitriolus' refers to the pitted texture on the holotype that resembles damage caused by sulphuric acid.
This creature coexisted with Makrodactylus, Skiphosoura, and Rhamphodactylus, which are likely close relatives.
It shares anatomical features with Skiphosoura, including tooth shape and spacing, a strongly curved pteroid bone, and robust mandibles and femurs.
However, Laueropterus differs from Skiphosoura by having a proportionally longer and shallower snout and a less conspicuous premaxillary crest.
Hone assigned the animal to Monofenestrata based on its large skull with a single nasoantorbital fenestra and long neck vertebrae.
Short metacarpals and first wing phalanges indicate that Laueropterus falls outside the clade Pterodactyloidea.
Laueropterus lived during the Late Jurassic period, specifically in the Tithonian age within the Mörnsheim Formation of Germany.
